subsection.title: Solution Strategy
subsection.description: - Work backward from the approved Desired Business Impact and propose the smallest product-level approach the user can try. - Present the proposal for revision or approval instead of asking the user to design the solution from scratch. - After the text strategy, include a `Product Context Diagram` with exactly one Mermaid `C4Context` diagram. - Generate the diagram from the approved Overview and the complete Section 2 draft. Show the target user, the PoC system, relevant external systems, and their relationships at product-role level. - Keep the text strategy independently reviewable. The diagram supplements the product intent, scope, values, and rules rather than replacing them. - Do not use `C4Container`, lower C4 levels, APIs, databases, deployment units, libraries, code structure, or implementation layers. - Include a permission, privacy, safety, limit, or failure rule only when the PoC itself must honor it. - Do not assign Feature IDs or add implementation detail.
subsection.example:
The product provides a short, controllable English conversation rehearsal for workers preparing for a high-stakes overseas business situation.
#### Product Context Diagram
```mermaid C4Context title Product Context for English Conversation Practice
Person(worker, "Worker", "Rehearses an upcoming overseas business conversation") System(practiceService, "English Practice Service", "Provides adaptive conversation practice and a visible completion state")
Rel(worker, practiceService, "Practices a selected work conversation with") ```

subsection.title: Essential User Experiences
subsection.description: - Propose every user experience the first PoC must not omit. - Give each essential experience a distinct name, user-observable result, and contribution to the Desired Business Impact. Explain how to recognize a result that meets that intent, rather than merely the presence of output. - When improvement is relevant, propose a useful signal and actively consider a tension metric that exposes harm from over-optimizing it. Keep these in the experience text, without mandatory metric columns or one metric per experience. If no meaningful metric fits, omit it or use an observable counterexample; do not block completion. - Distinguish optional monitoring signals from confirmed required conditions. A higher primary score cannot offset a required product, safety or permission violation. Do not invent thresholds or require a sample-size or evaluator-design exercise. - Make that contribution useful for judgment: show whose problem and outcome the experience serves, retaining supplied priorities and scope so later details do not pursue a different purpose. Do not invent policy, exclusions, or a separate intent field. - Do not require a starting condition, user-action sequence, screen flow, or demo procedure; Section 4 owns those execution choices. - Preserve confirmed values, permissions, limits, and failure guarantees when they affect whether an experience is complete. - Use only user-visible or otherwise directly observable results. Do not use implementation functions, internal state, technical layers, or subjective impressions.
subsection.example:
**Essential user experiences: Rehearse a high-stakes work conversation**
| Essential user experience | User-observable result | Business impact contribution | |---------------------------|------------------------|------------------------------| | Topic-specific practice begins | An AI instructor presents an opening question for the selected work situation | The learner can rehearse the conversation that currently causes difficulty | | The conversation adapts to the learner | After an English answer, a relevant English response and next question are visible | The learner can continue realistic practice instead of memorizing a fixed script | | The learner controls the session | Choosing to end stops the conversation; a completion message followed by more questions does not satisfy this result | The practice fits the learner's limited preparation time |
If practice completion is later optimized, consider completion rate alongside off-topic or repetitive questions as monitoring signals. No numeric target is set by this example. The learner's confirmed ability to end the session remains required regardless of those signals.
